content: Benjamin Franklin was one of the most influential Founding Fathers of the United States. He was a polymath who excelled in various fields, including writing, printing, satire, political theory, science, invention, civic activism, statesmanship, and diplomacy. As a scientist, Franklin made significant contributions to the Enlightenment and the history of physics, particularly through his discoveries and theories about electricity. He invented the lightning rod, bifocal glasses, the Franklin stove, a carriage odometer, and a musical instrument. Franklin also established the first public lending library in America and the first fire department in Pennsylvania. Franklin was an early advocate for colonial unity and played a pivotal role in shaping the concept of an American nation. As a diplomat during the American Revolution, he secured the French alliance, which was crucial for achieving independence. Born in Boston, Massachusetts, Franklin learned the printing trade from his older brother and became a successful newspaper editor, printer, and merchant in Philadelphia. He gained wealth and fame through his publications, including Poor Richard's Almanack and the Pennsylvania Gazette. His scientific experiments earned him international recognition. Franklin was instrumental in founding the University of Pennsylvania and Franklin & Marshall College. He was also the first president of the American Philosophical Society. He became a national hero for his efforts to repeal the unpopular Stamp Act and was widely admired in France as the American minister to Paris, fostering positive Franco-American relations. Franklin served as Postmaster General under the Continental Congress and later as President of the Supreme Executive Council of Pennsylvania. Toward the end of his life, he became a prominent abolitionist. Franklin's legacy as a scientist, inventor, and statesman has been celebrated for over two centuries. His image appears on currency, and his name is associated with numerous towns, counties, educational institutions, and cultural references. His father, Josiah Franklin, was a tallow chandler, and his mother, Abiah Folger, was the daughter of a miller and schoolteacher. Franklin was the fifteenth of seventeen children. Although his formal education ended at age ten, he continued to educate himself through extensive reading. At age 12, Franklin apprenticed with his brother James, a printer. He later wrote under the pseudonym Mrs. Silence Dogood, gaining popularity for his satirical letters. After a falling out with his brother, Franklin ran away to Philadelphia at age 17, where he worked in various printing shops. He eventually traveled to London, where he worked as a compositor before returning to Philadelphia in 1726. In 1727, Franklin founded the Junto, a group of like-minded individuals dedicated to self-improvement and community betterment. This group led to the creation of the Library Company of Philadelphia, the first subscription library in America. Franklin's printing business flourished, and he became the publisher of The Pennsylvania Gazette. He used the newspaper to advocate for local reforms and initiatives. Despite his success, Franklin remained humble, often signing his letters as B. Franklin, Printer. He was initiated into the Freemasons in 1731 and became a Grand Master in 1734. He published the first Masonic book in the Americas and remained a Freemason throughout his life. In 1730, Franklin entered a common-law marriage with Deborah Read. Together, they raised Franklin's illegitimate son, William, and had two children of their own, Francis Folger Franklin and Sarah Franklin. Deborah never accompanied Franklin on his trips to Europe due to her fear of the sea. Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanack, published under the pseudonym Richard Saunders, became widely popular for its wit and wisdom. He also wrote The Way to Wealth, a collection of adages and advice. As an inventor, Franklin created the lightning rod, the glass harmonica, bifocal glasses, and the flexible urinary catheter. He also charted the Gulf Stream and contributed to the understanding of ocean currents. Franklin founded the American Philosophical Society in 1743 to promote scientific discussion. His experiments with electricity, including the famous kite experiment, demonstrated that lightning is a form of electricity. He invented the lightning rod to protect buildings from lightning strikes. Franklin's public life included founding the Union Fire Company, one of the first volunteer firefighting companies in America, and printing innovative anti-counterfeiting currency for New Jersey. He played a key role in establishing the Academy and College of Philadelphia, which later became the University of Pennsylvania. Franklin also helped establish Pennsylvania Hospital, the first hospital in what would become the United States. Franklin's political career included serving as a councilman, Justice of the Peace, and member of the Pennsylvania Assembly. He was appointed joint deputy postmaster-general of North America and reformed the postal system. Franklin's diplomatic efforts included representing the colonies in England and later securing French support during the American Revolution. He opposed the Stamp Act and testified before the House of Commons, leading to its repeal. Franklin's writings and advocacy made him a leading spokesman for American interests in England. Franklin's contributions to science, politics, and society have left an enduring legacy. His work in electricity earned him the Royal Society's Copley Medal, and he was elected a Fellow of the Society. The CGS unit of electric charge, the franklin, is named in his honor. Franklin's observations on meteorology and refrigeration further demonstrated his scientific curiosity and ingenuity. His musical talents included playing the violin, harp, and guitar, and he invented an improved version of the glass harmonica. Franklin's efforts to improve society extended to organizing the local militia during Pontiac's Rebellion and advocating for fair treatment of Native Americans. He led the anti-proprietary party in Pennsylvania and was elected Speaker of the Pennsylvania House. Although he faced political setbacks, Franklin's influence on the American Revolution and the founding of the United States remains unparalleled.
